title: Complexity and Recursion Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on asymptotic notation, growth rates and amortised analysis, then the call stack, recursion design, recurrences with the Master theorem, and tail recursion with stack overflow.

chapters.title: Asymptotic Notation and Growth Rates
points: Big-O f(n)=O(g(n)): f ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0, an upper bound, usually quoted for the worst case
Omega is the lower bound (f ≥ c·g) and Theta is a tight bound, true only when both O and Omega hold
Drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n²+5n+9 is Theta(n²); different input variables stay separate, e.g. O(a+b)
Growth order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!
Big-O is not the same as worst case: it bounds a function, and best, average and worst case are separate functions each with own O, Omega and Theta

chapters.title: Analysing Loops and Amortised Cost
points: Single loop to n is O(n); nested loops multiply, so two loops to n give O(n²); sequential loops add and the larger term wins
A loop where i doubles or halves each step is O(log n); binary search is O(log n)
Amortised cost is the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence, with no probability involved
Dynamic array append: doubling capacity makes n appends cost O(n) total, so O(1) amortised, though one resize is O(n)
Amortised is not average case: it holds for every sequence, while average case assumes an input distribution; hash table resize is another amortised example

chapters.title: The Call Stack and Recursion Anatomy
points: Each call pushes a stack frame holding parameters, local variables and the return address; returning pops it
Recursion needs a base case that returns directly and a recursive case that moves strictly toward it
Calls unwind in last-in first-out order; factorial(3) pushes 3, 2, 1 then multiplies while popping
Recursion depth d costs O(d) stack space, even if no extra data structure is used
Missing or unreachable base case causes infinite recursion, e.g. n-2 skipping a base case of 0 when n is odd

chapters.title: Recursion Trees and Recurrences
points: A recurrence T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) has a subproblems of size n/b and f(n) work to split and combine
Recursion tree method: sum the work per level, multiplied by the number of levels, which is log_b n for balanced splits
Merge sort: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n gives n work on each of log n levels, so Theta(n log n)
Naive Fibonacci: T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+1 is exponential, about O(2ⁿ), because subproblems repeat; memoisation reduces it to O(n)
Linear recursion T(n)=T(n-1)+1 is O(n), and T(n)=T(n-1)+n is O(n²)

chapters.title: Master Theorem
points: Applies to T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) with a ≥ 1, b > 1; compare f(n) with n^(log_b a)
Case 1: f(n) polynomially smaller than n^(log_b a), so T=Theta(n^(log_b a)); binary tree leaves dominate
Case 2: f(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)), so T=Theta(n^(log_b a) · log n); merge sort gives Theta(n log n)
Case 3: f(n) polynomially larger, plus regularity condition, so T=Theta(f(n)); T=2T(n/2)+n² gives Theta(n²)
Does not apply to T(n-1) style recurrences or to gaps like n log n against n; binary search T=T(n/2)+1 is Case 2, Theta(log n)

chapters.title: Tail Recursion, Stack Overflow and Cheat Sheet
points: Tail call: the recursive call is the last action, with nothing left to do after it returns, e.g. fact(n-1, acc*n)
Tail call optimisation reuses the frame for O(1) stack space, but Python and Java do not do it; Scheme guarantees it and some C compilers do it
Stack overflow comes from unbounded or very deep recursion; fix by adding a base case, using a loop, or an explicit stack
Convert tail recursion to a loop by turning parameters into variables, and avoid deep recursion on large input such as a 10⁵ long list
Cheat sheet: O/Omega/Theta = upper/lower/tight; log n binary search; n log n sorts; amortised append O(1); Master theorem compares f(n) with n^(log_b a); recursion space = depth
